items.title: Jack DeJohnette — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I think playing with Miles, with Dave Holland, Chick Corea and Wayne was a very exciting period.

ctx.x: History Interview with NEA Jazz Master Jack DeJohnette. Now in his other studio, his recording studio! So Jack, when we left off yesterday we were talking about you joining the Miles Davis group. So, hopefully we can talk about some of that experience, because obviously that’s one the ones that really got you into the public, as everybody else who played with Miles launches their career into the public domain. Do you want to talk about the very first sessions that you were on? I think that’s where we left off. We…

Yeah. The time I spent was maybe three years, two or three years. It was kind of like a blur in a way. I think playing with Miles, with Dave Holland, Chick Corea and Wayne was a very exciting period. We always couldn’t wait to get on the bandstand to see what kind of mischief we could get into. In the studios… I get asked this question, “What was it like in the studio with Miles?” Especially during the period when he was doing In A Silent Way and Bitches Brew. Miles was in a very highly creative period where he…

would also be like Benny Maupin and Wayne. It was a flowing, organic session that Teo later edited and spliced together the best parts to sort of give it kind of a storyline, for lack of a better word. Miles had a penchant whenever he recorded, he recorded tempos, things that were slow because when he played these same tunes live they were always much faster. The studio versions were more relaxed. items.title: Jack DeJohnette interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 7, 2025
items.q: And then we had Dave Holland, we had Colin Wolcott, what’s his name — Trilok Gurtu So there were a lot of current musicians that were like on the faculty teaching there.

ctx.x: You had an association with Karl Berger and the Creative Music Studio. Can you tell me how that came about and how you think about your contributions to that now, in retrospect?

I think Karl Berger, I think Ornette has something to do with that. I just came and did some teaching with the students. And then we had Dave Holland, we had Colin Wolcott, what’s his name — Trilok Gurtu So there were a lot of current musicians that were like on the faculty teaching there. And so you know the challenge was for us, when we first started, was to play — to get the musicians who were at different levels of being able to play. Some couldn’t even play scales. Some — and so we had to try to figure out a…

He said an interesting thing that, he said, “Playing free requires more discipline, more stringent than anybody can tell me from the outside. The more precise you get, the more free you are.” And I remember when he said that I just like — wow — that if you observe it and listen to it you may get the impression that people are just playing randomly and that’s not what he’s about at all.
